title: Gave and taken (Job 1:20–22)
hookLine: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away"
carry: naked came I out of my mother's womb

cards: A messenger runs up to Job. Raiders came and took the oxen and the donkeys and killed the servants, "and I only am escaped alone to tell thee."
While he's still speaking, a second: fire fell from the sky and burned up the sheep. While he's still speaking, a third: raiders took the camels. While he's still speaking, a fourth.
Your sons and daughters were eating together in their oldest brother's house, and a great wind came from the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on them. They're dead.
The text gives no pause between the messengers. It all lands at once.

teach.h: HE TEARS HIS ROBE AND FALLS.
teach.b: Watch what Job does, in order. "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped." Grief comes first, and it's physical, and the book doesn't hurry him past it.
Jewish mourners still tear a garment at a death; the tearing is called keriah.

teach.h: NAKED CAME I, NAKED SHALL I RETURN.
teach.b: Only then, from the ground, Job speaks: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."
Everything I had was given; none of it was mine to keep. And still, from the floor, a blessing. Not instead of grief, but in the middle of it, with the robe already torn.

teach.h: THE LORD GAVE, AND THE LORD HATH TAKEN AWAY.
teach.b: The narrator adds one line: "In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly." The adversary said Job would curse God to his face. He doesn't.
Tradition put Job's words into the Jewish burial service, so mourners say this line at the graveside. Some find it a comfort; some find it almost impossible to say.
Both are honest, and the book has room for both, because this isn't Job's last word. He'll have much more to say, and not all of it gentle. Today, this is where he kneels.

how: Jewish mourners tear a garment, called keriah, when they learn of a close relative's death, and Job's words, the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away, are part of the traditional Jewish burial service.

o: tearing a garment in mourning, as Job did
the blessing mourners say over a new grave
shaving the head as a sign of a fresh start

games.q: Job hears the news — tap the pairs.
p: the mourner's tearing of a garment

s: Job blesses God before he grieves
first he tears his robe, shaves his head and falls to the ground. then he speaks.
the messengers arrive one after another, without a break
each comes while the one before is still speaking.
"the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away" is Job's last word on his suffering
it's his first. he'll have much more to say, and not all of it gentle.

games.q: you're Job. four messengers, one after another, and the last says your children are dead. what do you do?
o: curse God, just as the adversary said you would.
tear your robe, fall to the ground, and bless the name of the LORD.
games.why: he grieves with his whole body first, then from the ground says: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.

practice: Let one loss come to mind, a person, a home, a job, a friendship, a life you thought you'd have, and let it sit beside you, the way Job sat on the ground, with nothing to solve.

Breathe in and notice it was given; breathe out and notice it was taken, and you don't have to bless anything. If you pray, and the words fit today, you can say Job's line; if they don't, the silence is enough.

wordCard.voice: keriah, the Jewish mourning custom of tearing a garment at death, which Job did before he spoke a word. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: he gave; the verb in Job's line, the LORD gave, in Job 1:21.

carryVoice: Your line: naked came I out of my mother's womb. Grief first, then the words. That's day eight hundred thirty-nine.
